research_text:
# Research brief

## 1. API and reported finding

`javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec` represents a raw secret key independently of a provider. It constructs a `SecretKey` from a byte array without a `SecretKeyFactory`; Oracle says it is useful for raw keys representable as bytes without associated key parameters. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

The reported finding identifies the **first argument**, `keyMaterial`, of the four-argument constructor. That constructor copies `len` bytes beginning at `offset` and associates them with the supplied algorithm. The diagnostic says the analyzer did not observe the material as having been prepared by `Key.getEncoded()`. It is an observation about provenance, not a statement in the Java API contract. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

`Key.getEncoded()` returns a key’s primary encoded form, or `null` when the key does not support encoding. Oracle does **not** require every `SecretKeySpec` input to come from that method; its JCA guide also illustrates construction from existing raw key data. The CrySL file itself does not mention `Key.getEncoded()`, so the connection between that diagnostic and a CrySL predicate requires detector-implementation evidence. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html

## 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

- The four-argument constructor requires a non-null, non-empty array, a non-null algorithm name, and a valid slice. It reports insufficient material with `IllegalArgumentException` and negative offset or length with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. It copies the selected bytes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))
- The constructor **does not validate** that the bytes form a suitable key for the named algorithm. Oracle recommends an algorithm-specific key specification where such checks are needed, using `DESKeySpec` as its example. The `DESKeySpec` documentation separately provides `isWeak()` for testing DES material; its constructor documentation does not say that construction itself performs that weak-key test. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))
- For generating new secret keys, `KeyGenerator` is the documented API. Oracle recommends explicitly initializing it rather than relying on provider-specific defaults. Oracle also advises `SecureRandom`, rather than `java.util.Random`, for security-sensitive randomness. These are general API options, **not a prescribed fix for this particular diagnostic**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))

The reviewed official sources do not prescribe a universal remediation for the detector message or say that calling `getEncoded()` makes otherwise unsuitable key material suitable.

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/DESKeySpec.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Random.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

`SecretKeySpec` has been available since Java 1.4. Its `getFormat()` reports `"RAW"`, and its `getEncoded()` returns the key material in a new array. Oracle’s JCA guide describes `SecretKeySpec` as a provider-independent way to represent the **same key material**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

The reviewed documentation does **not** specify a general persisted-data or wire-format migration for changing key provenance, nor does it guarantee compatibility if the key material or algorithm changes. A new generated key is a new key, not a documented conversion of the old one. The `Key` documentation also warns that serialized keys may contain sensitive information. Provider and algorithm support must be checked against the relevant platform release and provider documentation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

Thus, compatibility and any migration path remain unresolved without the formats, algorithms, providers, and platform versions involved.

## 4. Exact matching rule in the supplied CrySL source

The source’s matching and ordering clauses are: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec
```

```text
EVENTS
	c1: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, keyAlgorithm);
	c2: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, offset, len, keyAlgorithm);
	Con := c1 | c2;

ORDER
	Con
```

The declared object types are `byte[]` for `keyMaterial`, `String` for `keyAlgorithm`, and `int` for `offset` and `len`. The event patterns specify **two- and four-parameter constructor calls**, respectively, under the named `SPEC`; they are not an unrestricted parameter-list pattern. The file does not specify a separate receiver-type pattern or subtype-matching semantics. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

The file states these constraints and requirement: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

```text
CONSTRAINTS
	keyAlgorithm in {"AES", "HmacSHA256", "HmacSHA384", "HmacSHA512"};
	length[keyMaterial] >= offset + len;
	neverTypeOf[keyMaterial, java.lang.String];

REQUIRES
	preparedKeyMaterial[keyMaterial] || randomized[keyMaterial];
```

It also declares `speccedKey[this, _]` and `generatedKey[this, keyAlgorithm]` under `ENSURES`. The source does not define how the required predicates are produced or propagated, or how `offset` and `len` are bound for `c1`. Its algorithm list is a rule constraint, not a list of all algorithms the Java API permits. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

**A name-only match is not stated by this rule.** It specifies constructor-event patterns under `javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec`, not a clause matching any method that merely shares the name. The file alone does not document the detector’s implementation, so it cannot conclusively rule out such matching by a particular implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

Rule source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl
